questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Poisoning & envenomation: emergency management
questions.stem: The antidote for organophosphate poisoning is:
questions.concept: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing the muscarinic DUMBBELS features with miosis, bronchorrhoea and fasciculations. Atropine reverses muscarinic effects and pralidoxime reactivates the enzyme if given before ageing.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Poisoning & envenomation: emergency management
questions.stem: The end point of atropinisation in organophosphate poisoning is:
options: Drying of secretions with clear chest and heart rate above 80
questions.concept: Atropine is titrated to drying of bronchial secretions, a clear chest and adequate heart rate - not to pupil size, which is an unreliable end point. Under-atropinisation from fear of toxicity is a common fatal error.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Poisoning & envenomation: emergency management
questions.stem: A patient with a haemotoxic snake bite has 20-minute whole blood clotting time that is prolonged. The essential treatment is:
options: Incision and suction of the bite
questions.concept: A prolonged 20-minute whole blood clotting test indicates systemic envenomation by a viper and mandates polyvalent antivenom. Tourniquets and incision are harmful and are no longer recommended.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Poisoning & envenomation: emergency management
questions.stem: The characteristic feature of neurotoxic (cobra or krait) envenomation is:
options: Descending paralysis with ptosis and respiratory failure
questions.concept: Elapid venom blocks the neuromuscular junction, producing ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, bulbar palsy and then respiratory paralysis with minimal local reaction, especially in krait bite which is often painless and nocturnal. Ventilation plus antivenom is life-saving.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Poisoning & envenomation: emergency management
questions.stem: Methanol poisoning is treated with:
options: Fomepizole or ethanol with sodium bicarbonate and haemodialysis
questions.concept: Methanol is metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to formic acid, causing high anion gap acidosis and blindness. Fomepizole or ethanol competitively blocks the enzyme, and haemodialysis removes methanol and formate.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Poisoning & envenomation: emergency management
questions.stem: Cherry-red skin with a normal arterial oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry despite severe hypoxia suggests:
questions.concept: Carboxyhaemoglobin is misread as oxyhaemoglobin by pulse oximetry, so saturation appears normal; co-oximetry is needed. Treatment is high-flow or hyperbaric oxygen. Methaemoglobinaemia instead causes chocolate-brown blood and cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Poisoning & envenomation: emergency management
questions.stem: Gastric lavage is absolutely contraindicated in poisoning with:
options: Corrosive acids and alkalis or hydrocarbons
questions.concept: Lavage risks perforation with corrosives and aspiration pneumonitis with hydrocarbons such as kerosene. It is also of no benefit beyond one hour of ingestion and is now rarely performed.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Poisoning & envenomation: emergency management
questions.stem: Which poison is NOT adsorbed by activated charcoal?
questions.concept: Charcoal does not bind metals such as iron and lithium, alcohols, strong acids and alkalis or cyanide, because these are small, highly ionised or poorly adsorbable molecules. Multi-dose charcoal is useful for carbamazepine, theophylline, dapsone and phenobarbitone.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Poisoning & envenomation: emergency management
questions.stem: Urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate is used in poisoning with:
questions.concept: Alkalinising urine ionises weak acids such as salicylate and phenobarbitone, trapping them in the tubular lumen and enhancing excretion. Acidification is no longer used because of rhabdomyolysis risk.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Poisoning & envenomation: emergency management
questions.stem: The specific antidote for iron poisoning is:
questions.concept: Desferrioxamine chelates free iron and is excreted as ferrioxamine, turning urine vin-rose. Dimercaprol and edetate are used for arsenic and lead respectively.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Geriatrics, palliative care & end-of-life issues
questions.stem: The commonest cause of a fall in an elderly person is:
options: Multifactorial - gait instability, polypharmacy, visual impairment and environmental hazards
questions.concept: Falls in old age are almost always multifactorial, so assessment covers gait and balance, vision, cognition, postural blood pressure, footwear, home hazards and a full drug review. Falls are a leading cause of hip fracture and loss of independence.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Geriatric Medicine and Palliative Care

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Geriatrics, palliative care & end-of-life issues
questions.stem: Which drug class is most strongly implicated in falls and delirium in the elderly and appears on the Beers criteria?
questions.concept: The Beers criteria flag long-acting benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, first-generation antihistamines and typical antipsychotics as potentially inappropriate in older adults because of sedation, falls, delirium and urinary retention.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Geriatric Medicine and Palliative Care

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Geriatrics, palliative care & end-of-life issues
questions.stem: Delirium is distinguished from dementia principally by:
options: Acute onset with fluctuating course and impaired attention
questions.concept: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness with an underlying medical precipitant such as infection, drugs, retention or electrolyte disturbance, and is reversible; dementia is chronic and progressive with attention preserved until late.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Geriatric Medicine and Palliative Care

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Geriatrics, palliative care & end-of-life issues
questions.stem: Frailty in the elderly is best characterised by:
options: Reduced physiological reserve with weakness, slow gait, weight loss and exhaustion
questions.concept: Frailty is a state of reduced reserve across systems, operationalised by Fried criteria - unintentional weight loss, weakness, exhaustion, slow walking speed and low activity - predicting poor outcomes independent of specific disease.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Geriatric Medicine and Palliative Care

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Geriatrics, palliative care & end-of-life issues
questions.stem: The single most effective intervention to prevent pressure ulcers in a bedridden elderly patient is:
options: Frequent repositioning with pressure-redistributing support and skin care
questions.concept: Two-hourly repositioning with pressure-relieving mattresses, nutritional support and skin moisture control prevents ulceration over the sacrum, heels and ischial tuberosities. Antibiotics have no preventive role.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Geriatric Medicine and Palliative Care

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Geriatrics, palliative care & end-of-life issues
questions.stem: The principle of the analgesic ladder in cancer pain is:
options: Step from non-opioid to weak opioid to strong opioid, given by mouth and by the clock
Reserve opioids until the terminal week
Use intramuscular injections as first choice
questions.concept: The WHO ladder advises analgesia by mouth, by the clock and by the ladder, with adjuvants at every step. Regular dosing with breakthrough rescue doses controls pain far better than as-required administration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Geriatrics, palliative care & end-of-life issues
questions.stem: There is no ceiling dose for which analgesic in cancer pain?
questions.concept: Strong opioids such as morphine have no maximum dose - the correct dose is that which relieves pain without unacceptable toxicity - whereas paracetamol and NSAIDs have clear ceiling doses. Constipation must be prevented prophylactically with a laxative.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Geriatrics, palliative care & end-of-life issues
questions.stem: The commonest cause of death in patients with dementia in the terminal phase is:
questions.concept: Progressive dysphagia leads to aspiration pneumonia, the usual terminal event in advanced dementia. Tube feeding does not prevent aspiration or improve survival, which is central to advance care planning discussions.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Geriatric Medicine and Palliative Care

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Geriatrics, palliative care & end-of-life issues
questions.stem: An advance directive or living will primarily serves to:
options: Record a competent patient's wishes about future treatment should they lose capacity
questions.concept: An advance directive records treatment preferences made while competent, to guide care after loss of capacity. In India the Supreme Court recognised advance directives and passive withdrawal of futile life support in the Common Cause judgment of 2018; active euthanasia remains illegal.
questions.reference: Common Cause v Union of India (2018)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Geriatrics, palliative care & end-of-life issues
questions.stem: Polypharmacy in the elderly is best addressed by:
options: Structured medication review with deprescribing of drugs lacking clear indication
Adding a drug for each symptom
questions.concept: Systematic review against indication, benefit, interaction and life expectancy, followed by planned tapering of unnecessary drugs, reduces adverse events. Prescribing cascades - a drug given to treat another drug's side effect - should be identified.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Geriatric Medicine and Palliative Care

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Nutritional & vitamin deficiency states in adults
questions.stem: Wernicke encephalopathy results from deficiency of:
questions.concept: Thiamine deficiency, classically in alcoholics, causes the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. It is a medical emergency, and thiamine must be given before glucose because a glucose load can precipitate or worsen it.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Nutritional & vitamin deficiency states in adults
questions.stem: Pellagra is characterised by the triad of:
options: Bleeding gums and poor wound healing
questions.concept: Niacin deficiency causes the three Ds - photosensitive pigmented dermatitis with Casal necklace, diarrhoea and dementia. It occurs in maize-based diets, carcinoid syndrome and isoniazid therapy, since tryptophan is the niacin precursor.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Nutritional & vitamin deficiency states in adults
questions.stem: Isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy is prevented by supplementing:
questions.concept: Isoniazid forms hydrazones with pyridoxal phosphate and increases its urinary loss, so 10 mg of pyridoxine daily is given prophylactically. Pyridoxine is also the antidote for isoniazid overdose seizures.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Nutritional & vitamin deficiency states in adults
questions.stem: Bitot spots and conjunctival xerosis indicate deficiency of:
questions.concept: Vitamin A deficiency progresses from night blindness through conjunctival xerosis and Bitot spots to corneal xerosis, ulceration and keratomalacia, the leading preventable cause of childhood blindness.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Nutritional & vitamin deficiency states in adults
questions.stem: Scurvy is characterised by:
options: Perifollicular haemorrhage, swollen bleeding gums and impaired wound healing
questions.concept: Vitamin C is required for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation in collagen synthesis, so deficiency causes fragile capillaries with perifollicular haemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, gingival bleeding, subperiosteal haemorrhage and poor wound healing.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Nutritional & vitamin deficiency states in adults
questions.stem: Osteomalacia in an adult is most consistently associated with:
options: Low serum vitamin D with low or normal calcium, low phosphate and raised alkaline phosphatase
questions.concept: Defective mineralisation of mature bone gives bone pain, proximal myopathy with waddling gait and pseudofractures (Looser zones), with low 25-hydroxyvitamin D, secondary hyperparathyroidism and raised alkaline phosphatase.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Nutritional & vitamin deficiency states in adults
questions.stem: Which vitamin deficiency causes prolongation of the prothrombin time?
questions.concept: Vitamin K is the cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S, so deficiency prolongs the prothrombin time first because factor VII has the shortest half-life.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Nutritional & vitamin deficiency states in adults
questions.stem: Which mineral deficiency causes acrodermatitis enteropathica with poor wound healing, hypogeusia and diarrhoea?
questions.concept: Zinc deficiency, inherited or from malabsorption, parenteral nutrition or alcoholism, causes periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia, impaired taste, poor wound healing and immune dysfunction, and responds rapidly to zinc.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Nutritional & vitamin deficiency states in adults
questions.stem: Keshan disease, a dilated cardiomyopathy, results from deficiency of:
questions.concept: Selenium deficiency in low-selenium soil regions causes Keshan cardiomyopathy and Kashin-Beck osteoarthropathy; selenium is a cofactor for glutathione peroxidase and for deiodinases in thyroid hormone metabolism.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Nutritional & vitamin deficiency states in adults
questions.stem: Refeeding syndrome after nutritional rehabilitation of a severely malnourished adult is characterised by:
options: Hypophosphataemia with hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and thiamine deficiency
questions.concept: Reintroduction of carbohydrate drives insulin-mediated intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium, precipitating arrhythmias, cardiac failure and rhabdomyolysis. Feeding is started slowly with electrolyte monitoring and thiamine before calories.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: In normal pregnancy, plasma volume increases by approximately:
questions.concept: Plasma volume rises by about 40 to 50% while red cell mass rises only 20 to 30%, producing the physiological dilutional anaemia of pregnancy with a nadir haematocrit around 32 weeks.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Cardiac output in pregnancy peaks at:
options: Around 30 to 32 weeks and again immediately postpartum
questions.concept: Cardiac output rises about 40%, plateauing near 30 to 32 weeks, with a further sharp rise immediately after delivery due to autotransfusion from the contracting uterus - the period of greatest risk in cardiac disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: The acid-base picture of normal pregnancy is:
questions.concept: Progesterone-driven hyperventilation lowers arterial PCO2 to about 30 mmHg, giving a mild respiratory alkalosis with renal bicarbonate excretion in compensation, which facilitates fetal carbon dioxide transfer.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Which renal change is normal in pregnancy?
options: Glomerular filtration rate rises about 50 percent with a fall in serum creatinine
questions.concept: Renal plasma flow and GFR rise by up to 50%, so serum urea and creatinine fall; a creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL that would be normal outside pregnancy may indicate significant renal impairment in pregnancy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Fetal heart activity is first detectable by transvaginal ultrasound at about:
questions.concept: Cardiac activity is visible transvaginally at about 6 weeks when the crown-rump length reaches 5 mm; absence beyond 7 weeks with a gestational sac over 25 mm suggests early pregnancy failure.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Surfactant production reaches functional maturity at approximately:
questions.concept: Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant from about 24 weeks but adequate amounts appear by 34 to 36 weeks, which is why antenatal corticosteroids are given for anticipated delivery before 34 weeks. A lecithin-sphingomyelin ratio above 2 indicates maturity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Which structure carries oxygenated blood to the fetus?
questions.concept: The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus, while the paired umbilical arteries return deoxygenated blood. A single umbilical artery is associated with congenital anomalies.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Fetal haemoglobin has higher oxygen affinity than adult haemoglobin because it:
questions.concept: HbF, composed of two alpha and two gamma chains, interacts weakly with 2,3-DPG, shifting the oxygen dissociation curve to the left and favouring placental oxygen uptake from maternal blood.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology, Respiration

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Human chorionic gonadotropin peaks at approximately:
questions.concept: hCG doubles roughly every 48 hours in early pregnancy, peaks at 8 to 10 weeks and then declines to a plateau. Its function is to maintain the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over progesterone production at about 7 to 9 weeks.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Physiological changes in pregnancy include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: A fall in fibrinogen and clotting factors
questions.concept: Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state with raised fibrinogen and factors VII, VIII, IX and X and reduced protein S and fibrinolysis, explaining the increased thromboembolic risk. Tidal volume rises and functional residual capacity falls from diaphragmatic elevation.
